title: Final review guide
lead: Every page of the 2025 final review session, in order, turned into the question it asks, with an answer written from the decks. The deck also revisits earlier units on aphasia, the critical period, semantic blocking and speech perception. Predicted questions at the end change one thing in a review question.

items.q: What is orthographic depth, and how do English, Finnish and Korean differ?
items.a: Orthographic depth is how consistently a script's spelling matches pronunciation. English is a relatively deep script, because its irregular spellings, like COLONEL and PARADIGM, do not reliably give the sound. Finnish and Korean are very shallow scripts, and Pinyin for Mandarin and French are relatively regular.

items.q: Why is Finnish called a transparent or shallow script, and what does that mean for children?
items.a: Finnish is shallow because each letter corresponds more or less unambiguously to one phoneme. Doubled letters stand for geminated consonants or long vowels. So Finnish children learn to decode pronunciations for written forms very quickly.

items.q: How does learning to decode in English compare with other languages that use the Roman alphabet?
items.a: Children learn to decode more slowly in English, which is an outlier among these languages. In Grade 1, children learning many other languages generate plausible pronunciations for pseudowords at a much higher rate than English learners. This is because English spelling is deep and irregular.

items.q: Korean is even more regular than Finnish. What orthographic feature corresponds roughly to velar place of articulation?
items.a: The angular shape ㄱ corresponds roughly to velar place of articulation. Korean gives similar phonemes similar symbols, so the velar letters ㄱ, ㄲ and ㅋ share that shape. Doubling it or adding a stroke tells the related consonants apart.

items.q: What does the frequency by regularity interaction mean?
items.a: It means the frequency effect is much larger for exception words than for regular words. High-frequency words are named quickly whether they are regular or exceptions. Low-frequency exception words are much slower than low-frequency regular words. So regularity matters mostly for words we rarely see.

items.q: How does a dual-route interpretation explain the frequency by regularity interaction?
items.a: It proposes two separate processes, a sublexical decoding process and a lexical process for known words. For high-frequency words, the lexical process is so fast and efficient that decoding has little influence. Decoding only shows up for nonwords and low-frequency words, where its regularized answer slows down exception words.

items.q: How do the PDP models of Seidenberg and McClelland (1989) differ from dual-route models?
items.a: In PDP models, rules are just generalizations from many words, not a separate process. The lexicon is also distributed, with some whole-word information in the spelling to sound mappings and some elsewhere. The research strategy is to explain reading with domain-general learning, rather than reverse-engineer it from adult and patient data.

items.q: How did the PDP model capture the frequency by regularity interaction without separate processes?
items.a: Regular words are consistent with statistical patterns from many other words, while exception words are inconsistent with them. Frequency also affects how well each word is learned. So highly frequent words are less affected by inconsistency, and only rare exception words suffer badly.

items.q: How can a single route read both words and nonwords?
items.a: In principle, nonwords are named with the same set of weights used for words. Generalization takes advantage of the same statistical patterns that give rise to regularity effects. So no separate nonword route or rule system is needed.

items.q: The model's nonword accuracy was not very good. Was the theory wrong, or was the problem the way the model was made?
items.a: This is a classic case of ambiguity in model evaluation, because a failed simulation does not identify its own cause. The theory that one associative mechanism reads nonwords and exceptions could be wrong. Or the problem could be specific to how the model was built. The later work points to the model's phonological representations.

items.q: What does nonword reading have to do with phonological representations?
items.a: Many studies link decoding, or nonword reading, with phonological processing. Seidenberg and McClelland used odd phonological representations called Wickelfeatures. Plaut and colleagues (1996) improved the phonological representations and got better performance on nonwords.

items.q: How are phonological representations and nonword generalization related?
items.a: Generalization depends on similarity, a principle inherited from behaviorism. Poor phonological representations like Wickelfeatures fail to capture the similarity space of words, so generalization to nonwords suffers. Word-specific information is more robust because it does not depend entirely on generalization.

items.q: What did Harm and Seidenberg (1999) do, and what did they find?
items.a: Harm and Seidenberg (1999) manipulated the amount of noise in the model's phonological representations. The model replicated key findings on developmental dyslexia. The degree of phonological deficit was related to phonological dyslexia, and word recognition was relatively spared.

items.q: How is Pinker and Ullman's (2002) dual-route model of the past tense similar to the dual-route model of reading, and how is it different?
items.a: Both separate word-specific knowledge from a productive operation. The past-tense lexicon looks up stored irregulars like held, while the grammar adds -ed to forms like walk. They differ in origin. The reading model came from patient double dissociations, while Pinker and colleagues were motivated by rule-based generative linguistics.

items.q: If the two architectures are similar, why do they have different origins?
items.a: The reading dual-route model was developed from neuropsychological double dissociations. Pinker and colleagues were motivated by other concerns. Generative linguistics of the time was mostly about categorical, symbolic, rule-based grammars, and those rules often have exceptions.

items.q: How does the dual-process model handle exceptions, and what properties does the exception process have?
items.a: It puts the exceptions in a second process, so the grammar can stay elegant, symbolic and categorical. That process has all the properties the rule route lacks. It is word-specific, sensitive to frequency of occurrence, and sensitive to phonological similarity, as in keep-kept, weep-wept and leap-leapt.

items.q: What alternative did Rumelhart and McClelland (1987) propose?
items.a: Rumelhart and McClelland (1987) proposed that the past tense is all associative learning. One network learns regular and irregular verbs together, with no add -ed rule. It encodes the root's sound as Wickelfeatures and maps them through modifiable connections onto the past-tense form.

items.q: What is U-shaped learning?
items.a: U-shaped learning is when children get worse before they get better. Some frequent irregular verbs, like run-ran, are learned early. Then children spontaneously start producing regularizations like runned. Eventually they produce the correct forms again.

items.q: Why is U-shaped learning important to the Words and Rules approach?
items.a: The approach explains the U as distinct stages and processes. Early correct forms are just imitations. When the rule is learned, it is applied to all cases as the best hypothesis, which produces runned. Over time, exceptions are learned associatively one by one, and the blocking process develops.

items.q: How does Rumelhart and McClelland's model produce U-shaped learning?
items.a: The training set was based on data about input to children, which changes over time. Early on, irregular verbs predominate, because the highest-frequency verbs like GIVE, TAKE, HAVE and GO are irregular. As more regular verbs enter the vocabulary, the model reorganizes to capture them, and this interferes with some early-learned irregulars.

items.q: How could Rumelhart and McClelland run a wug test with real words?
items.a: The model was trained on only a small number of verbs, so many real verbs were new to it. Testing those untrained verbs worked like a wug test. The model got most Wickelfeatures right and produced many correct forms, such as shaped and typed.

items.q: What was the problem with some of the model's outputs?
items.a: Some outputs were forms people would never say, such as membled for mail and toureder for tour. The authors admitted that humans are unlikely to make these errors. Prince and Pinker (1988) argued that feature-only representations blend competing past tenses into these hybrids.

items.q: What is the theoretical premise of Joanisse and Seidenberg's (1999) model?
items.a: Rule-like generalization is supported by phonological representations. Irregular forms require greater support from semantics. The model links speech input, semantics and speech output in one system instead of using separate routes.

items.q: What target phenomenon was Joanisse and Seidenberg's model built to explain?
items.a: It was built to explain the dissociation between irregular and nonword past tense in neuropsychological data. Some patients are worst on nonwords, and others are worst on irregulars. Damage to phonology should hurt nonwords most, and damage to semantics should hurt irregulars most.

items.q: What past-tense problems do Broca's aphasia patients have?
items.a: Broca's aphasia patients have problems with regular morphology, especially nonwords like wug-wugged and blick-blicked. They have injury to left anterior brain regions and poor speech production. When phonology is impaired in the model, it shows the same pattern, with nonwords worst.

items.q: Which patients have problems with irregulars?
items.a: Wernicke's and Alzheimer's patients are poor on irregulars. So are anomic patients with injury to inferior or middle temporal brain regions. Their irregular scores are clearly lower than their regular and nonword scores, which matches semantic damage in the model.

items.q: What is the attractive dichotomy between Wernicke's and Broca's aphasia?
items.a: Wernicke's aphasia produces word salad or Jabberwocky, often with neologisms, while syntax stays roughly intact. Broca's aphasia produces telegraphic speech, with difficulty with word order and grammatical particles. Important content words are relatively spared in Broca's aphasia.

items.q: Why is it confusing to call Broca's original patients Broca's aphasics?
items.a: Broca's actual patients would not necessarily be classified as Broca's aphasics. They were arguably unable to produce speech at all, apparently because of motor control problems. Today they would be classified as having apraxia of speech, not a grammar problem.

items.q: Why is the dichotomy of lexicon problems in Wernicke's aphasia and grammar problems in Broca's aphasia so appealing?
items.a: It lines up with a sharp distinction between the grammar and the lexicon in late 20th century formal linguistics. That distinction starts with Chomsky's framing of the computational problem of language learning. It also rests on demonstrations that syntax is independent of semantics, as in “colorless green ideas sleep furiously”.

items.q: How do the functional and positional levels of speech production relate to the lexicon and grammar dichotomy?
items.a: At the functional level, lemmas have an arbitrary relationship to their referents, like the lexicon. At the positional level, syntactic trees and affixes come from abstract syntactic processes, like grammar. Compounds like HOUSEBOAT seem non-arbitrary, but speech errors like “easy enoughly” show derivational morphology happens at the positional level.

items.q: How does Tzeltal talk about nearby space, compared with most languages?
items.a: Most languages talk about nearby space egocentrically, using left, right, in front and behind. Tzeltal, a Western Mayan language spoken in Chiapas, uses absolute directions instead. A small number of mostly unrelated languages, in places such as Bali and Queensland, do the same.

items.q: Why is Tzeltal's uphill and downhill system an absolute system?
items.a: Tzeltal's system is historically landmark-based, so things are uphill or downhill from one another. But uphill and downhill are used as cardinal directions, not as left or right of the speaker. Because these directions stay fixed when the speaker turns, the system is absolute.

items.q: What is the non-linguistic chips task of Majid and colleagues (2004), and what did it find?
items.a: A participant sees a card on one table, waits, is rotated 180 degrees, and picks the matching card at a second table. A relative choice keeps the arrangement fixed to the body, and an absolute choice keeps it fixed to the environment. Dutch speakers were overwhelmingly relative, and Tzeltal speakers were mostly absolute.

items.q: How can the rotation task be extended to spatial inference?
items.a: Participants learn one spatial relation at one display, rotate, and learn a second relation that shares an object. They then place an object using both relations together. Relative and absolute coding lead to different placements, and Dutch and Tzeltal speakers again follow their preferred frames.

items.q: What alternative explanation did Li and Gleitman raise?
items.a: Li and Gleitman pointed out that Tzeltal speakers were tested outside, with visible and familiar landmarks. Typical psychology lab studies are done in windowless rooms. So the language difference could come from the testing environment instead of the language.

items.q: What did Li and Gleitman find when they changed the environment for English speakers?
items.a: With the blinds down, English speakers overwhelmingly used relative position, like the Dutch speakers in earlier studies. With the blinds up and a view of the street, or outdoors, their relative preference was less pronounced. So the environment, not only the language, affects which frame people use.

items.q: Why were Levinson and colleagues not impressed with Li and Gleitman's study?
items.a: They claimed Li and Gleitman made it too obvious that the study was about rotation. Li and Gleitman reduced memory load and the time and distance between stimulus and test. Their participants were also Ivy League students, who excel at figuring out what the experimenter wants.

items.q: Is there categorical perception for the dimensions of sign language, and how would you test it?
items.a: Categorical perception is tested by changing a sign feature in steps and measuring identification and discrimination. One hand configuration continuum crosses a phonemic contrast between please and sorry. The other makes only an allophonic change that does not change the sign.

items.q: What did the identification and discrimination curves for sign show?
items.a: For the phonemic contrast, there was a fairly sharp categorical boundary between stimuli 4 and 6. That boundary matched the peak in the discrimination function. For the allophonic condition, identification was much shallower, with many more ambiguous stimuli, and there was no discrimination peak.

items.q: How is brain activity during sign comprehension similar to and different from spoken language?
items.a: It is similar because it is left-lateralized and uses the classical language areas. These are Broca's area in inferior frontal cortex and Wernicke's area in posterior superior temporal cortex. It differs because sign shows more activity in visual areas and less in auditory areas. Sign also activates superior parietal cortex, which holds classic spatial areas.

items.q: What do we know about sign language from these studies?
items.a: Sign language has phonological structure, and native signers show categorical perception for some contrastive features. Learning a signed language reorganizes the brain, especially the lateralization of motion processing. Only deaf signers show enhanced attention in the visual periphery. Compared with tic-tac, signed sentences activate posterior superior temporal cortex, which is Wernicke's area.

items.q: Which version of the critical period hypothesis fits the data of Johnson and Newport (1989) better? Does this change our reading of the L1 critical period data?
items.a: Johnson and Newport (1989) see the maturational state hypothesis as more consistent with their data. Their second-language learners had already exercised their language ability on a first language, yet later starters still learned less well. This does change the L1 interpretation, because late first-language learners never exercised the ability. So both versions predict their poor outcomes, and L1 data cannot tell the versions apart.

items.q: What did Mayberry, Lock and Kazmi (2002) find about early language and later learning?
items.a: Deaf children who first meet a language, ASL, at ages 9 to 15 have difficulty learning it. Children who went deaf after first learning a spoken language do much better, and these differences persist into adulthood. Adults with early signed or early spoken language performed equally well, so what matters is having some language early.

items.q: What if the semantic blocking effect arises at the level of visual object recognition?
items.a: Two responses rule this out. First, the stimuli were normed so that same-category objects were not more visually similar, on average, than objects from different categories. Second, a control experiment blocked by visual similarity and found different results, with the effect already in the first block. So the semantic blocking effect is not likely to come from visual similarity.

items.q: Hermens and colleagues found no blocking effect with objects shown simultaneously. How did Belke and colleagues address this?
items.a: Belke and colleagues asked participants to view displays of four items simultaneously and produce their names in serial. This tested whether something about seeing objects one at a time caused the effect. All the objects were visible at once, but the names still had to be produced one after another.

items.q: Why did Belke and colleagues measure eye movements during naming?
items.a: Eye movements give separate timing measures for different stages of naming. Gaze duration is how long the eyes stay on an object. Eye-speech lag is the time between leaving an object and starting to say its name, so each measure can track a different stage.

items.q: Where does the semantic blocking effect appear, and what does that say about its stage?
items.a: The blocking effect appears in gaze duration, but only after the first cycle, which points to lemma selection. Overall speech duration decreases over the experiment but shows no blocking effect, so the gesture level is not involved. Eye-speech lag shows no significant effect, so phonological encoding is not involved either.

items.q: Is phoneme identification for word recognition more like thresholded or cascaded processing, and how did McMurray, Tanenhaus, Aslin and Spivey (2003) test it?
items.a: In thresholded processing, like a lumber mill, only a finished phoneme category is passed on. In cascaded processing, like a food web, graded information flows on before the decision is complete. McMurray, Tanenhaus, Aslin and Spivey (2003) tested a /b/ to /p/ continuum in a visual world display while tracking eye movements.

items.q: What did participants' mouse choices between the bear and the pear look like?
items.a: Participants used the mouse to click the image most consistent with what they heard. Their choices formed a typical step-like identification function across voice onset time. Short VOTs gave bear and long VOTs gave pear.

items.q: What did the eye movements reveal that the mouse choices did not?
items.a: Eye movements revealed that ambiguity is gradient. There were more looks to the competitor when the sound was close to the category boundary, even within one chosen category. So fine phonetic detail reaches word recognition, which supports cascaded processing.

items.q: How do competitor looks change with distance from the category boundary?
items.a: Competitor looks rise as a sound gets closer to the category boundary, from either side. For bear responses, looks to the pear rise as VOT moves toward the boundary. For pear responses, looks to the bear rise the same way, in both early and late time windows.

items.q: How does English pseudoword reading compare with other languages by Grade 4 rather than Grade 1?
items.a: By Grade 4, English learners read pseudowords almost as accurately as children learning most of the other languages. In Grade 1 they read only about half correctly, far below the others. So English children do learn to decode, but more slowly, because English spelling is deep.

items.q: In the dual-route view, why is a high-frequency exception word not slowed down?
items.a: A high-frequency exception word is not slowed because the lexical process is so fast and efficient. It produces the correct pronunciation before decoding can have much influence. So the regularized answer from decoding never gets a chance to compete.

items.q: In the triangle model, what happens to reading if semantics is damaged instead of phonology?
items.a: Damaging semantics produces a specific impairment on exception words, which is surface dyslexia. Plaut and colleagues (1996) found this after lesioning a simplified semantic system. Exception words need semantic support because their spelling to sound mapping conflicts with other words.

items.q: How would the Words and Rules account explain a child who says runned and later goes back to ran?
items.a: The account says the child learned the add -ed rule and applied it to every verb as the best hypothesis, producing runned. Over time, the child stores ran associatively in lexical knowledge. The blocking process develops, so the stored ran blocks the rule's runned.

items.q: Which kind of past tense should be hardest for a patient with phonological damage, according to Joanisse and Seidenberg?
items.a: Nonwords should be hardest, because they depend entirely on generalizing a sound pattern. Familiar regulars and irregulars still get support from their own training. This matches Broca's aphasia patients and the phonologically impaired model.

items.q: What would Levinson and colleagues predict for English speakers tested outdoors with four animals, a long delay and widely separated tables?
items.a: They would predict that the relative bias remains. Levinson and colleagues (2002) found that the bias is robust to the environment when there is a significant memory component. It also has to be unclear that the study is about rotation, and the harder version makes the rotation less salient.

items.q: Would hearing signers show enhanced peripheral visual attention like deaf signers?
items.a: No, enhanced peripheral attention is found only in deaf signers. Hearing signers do share the leftward shift of motion-perception areas, because that shift comes from learning sign. The peripheral enhancement may need deafness, because hearing people rely on sound for the far periphery.

items.q: Would a deaf adult who learned ASL from infancy learn English grammar later as well as someone with an early spoken language?
items.a: Yes, deaf adults who had ASL in infancy did as well on English grammar as hearing adults with an early spoken language. Adults with no early language did much worse, close to chance. So any early language, signed or spoken, supports later language learning.

items.q: What would a thresholded model predict for looks to the competitor across voice onset time?
items.a: A thresholded model predicts that competitor looks would not change with distance from the boundary inside a category. Only the finished category would be passed on, so every token heard as bear would act alike. McMurray and colleagues found more competitor looks near the boundary, which goes against this prediction.

items.q: Which kind of past tense should be hardest after semantic damage in Joanisse and Seidenberg's model?
items.a: Irregulars should be hardest after semantic damage, because irregular forms need greater support from semantics. Regulars and nonwords still get support from phonological patterns. The model's irregulars fell below regulars and nonwords, matching Wernicke's, Alzheimer's and anomic patients.
